posts.title: Law as a Business in Kenya
posts.author: Allan Ong’ato, Esq
posts.excerpt: By Allan Ong’ato, Esq. Law as a Business has long been distinguished from Law as a Profession. We examine that perceived distinction, and what it means in practice to run a law firm in Kenya: client accounts, the rules on marketing, and the charging of fees.
posts.body:
Law as a Business has sought to be distinguished from Law as a Profession. Extracts from an article by Champ S. Andrews titled “The Law: A Business or a Profession?”¹ attempt to draw the perceived distinction between the Law when it is practised as a Business and when it is practised as a Profession, set out as a conversation between a law student and a distinguished jurist. It states thus:

> But I would have the profession schools honest with the youthful enthusiast who knocks at their portals. I would have them say: choose between the law as a business and the law as a profession. If you decide on law as a business, then strip the calling of its arrogance and cant. Quit posing as a superior being, as a protector of the weak, as a man who prefers the reward of duty performed to services paid for.

> If the young man decides to enter it as a profession, let him be told of what severe stuff the heroes of the bar are made. Let him realise that the sacrifices he will make and the rewards he will achieve are utterly different from those of men in other walks of life. Do not let him expect to reap both the rewards of a business career and a professional one.

> It is a good thing for every man to be trained in the ways of the law; the years devoted to its study will not be wasted, even for those who conclude they are not heroic enough to become real professional lawyers, nor skilful enough as captains of industry to make law business pay. Training in law school will make better and broader men in whatever walk of life the student may go.

The article goes on to paint the picture of the law when it is practised as a business in the following terms:

> In older countries, England particularly, men have some independent income as a rule on entering the law, and under such circumstances it can be practised as a profession. In the United States ninety-nine out of a hundred lawyers practise it for all it is worth as a living… Anything to win is the motto; and with thousands of young men crowding the profession every year, where only a few are needed, there seems little hope that economic competition will leave the law anything but a sordid trade, based still on the false pretence that it is a dignified professional calling.

Law as a Business generally carries a poor perception among the general public. Many consider lawyers in business to be money-hungry, motivated by greed, and producing nothing. An article by Norman Bowie titled “The Law: From a Profession to a Business”² aptly describes this:

> The public believes that the practice of law has become a business, and that lawyers are in the profession for the money… Allegedly, lawyers overcharge, create work, and delay in order to make more money. In return they produce nothing useful; they do not make cars, steel, or heavy machinery. They are perceived by many as social parasites who make a handsome living off the productive labour of others.

> Traditionally, business has not been viewed as a profession. The chief characteristic that distinguishes it is the motivation of business people, who are perceived to be egoistic, their primary motivation, according to economic theory, being to maximise their self-interest. This lack of altruistic spirit is thought sufficient to distinguish business from the professions.

> Arguably, the competitive egoism of the market is better for the public than altruism. Adam Smith is the father of this view and Milton Friedman the most famous of his progeny. Business contributes to the public good whether or not it is considered a profession.

Norman Bowie argues that lawyers might apply the same rationale. If they give up the pretence of being altruistically motivated and admit that they are in it for the money, the public still benefits: self-interest causes zealous client advocacy, which in turn promotes legal justice. Through a kind of “invisible hand”, the clash of lawyers jealously advocating client interests, the appropriate decision is reached.

If the law is to remain a profession in the traditional sense, it must not lose its traditional mission. That is the danger in an era of specialisation, large firms, and association with corporate clients.³

The functions of the law are: to enable a large mass of diversified human beings to live together;⁴ to serve as a repository of society’s most cherished values; and to promote justice. Lawyers behave altruistically so long as they enter the profession, and make legal decisions, with an eye toward promoting human interaction, society’s cherished values, and justice.⁵

This having been said, Plato, in his famous work De Republica, reminds us that you can do good and still do well.⁶

## Law firms

In Kenya, law as a business is mostly undertaken through law firms. Only persons admitted as Advocates of the High Court of Kenya pursuant to the Advocates Act⁷ may register law firms and practise law on their own behalf in Kenya.⁸ One may register the firm as a sole proprietorship, as a partnership under the Partnerships Act,⁹ or as a Limited Liability Partnership under the Limited Liability Partnerships Act.¹⁰

Upon registering a firm, and before taking instructions from clients, every Advocate must purchase an insurance policy of not less than KES 1 million. Where practising in partnership or as a limited liability partnership, the professional indemnity cover is purchased in common.¹¹

That cover is used to compensate clients for loss or damage arising from claims in respect of any civil liability or breach of trust by the advocate or their employees.¹²

## Practising certificate

An Advocate is required to take out a practising certificate for every practice year, which runs from 1st January to 31st December.¹³

## Client account

An Advocate running a firm must keep a client account, one or several, as the Advocate thinks necessary.¹⁴ Its purpose is to hold all client money. It may be a current or deposit account at a bank, building society or financial institution as defined in the Banking Act,¹⁵ in the name of the advocate(s), but whose title contains either the word “client” or the word “trust”.

The Rules¹⁶ describe client money as:

> …money held or received by an advocate on account of a person for whom he is acting in relation to the holding or receipt of such money, either as an advocate or, in connexion with his practice, as agent, bailee, trustee, stakeholder or in any other capacity, including money held by way of deposit against fees to be earned or disbursements to be incurred, and money held on account of a trustee; but excluding money to which the only person entitled is the advocate, and money received in payment of an agreed fee.

An Advocate must, at all times, keep properly written-up books of account sufficient to show every receipt of client money for each separate client; every payment or application of it for each separate client; the amount held in the client account for each separate client; and the moneys expended for, and costs charged to, each separate client.¹⁷ These books include a cash book and a ledger, kept so as to separate client money dealt with through a client account from the advocate’s own money relating to clients’ affairs, together with a record of all bills of costs delivered, distinguishing profit costs from disbursements.¹⁸

Every advocate must preserve all required books of account for at least six years from the date of the last entry.¹⁹ Before the practising certificate of an Advocate who has handled client money is renewed, one requirement is an Accountant’s Certificate confirming that the Advocate’s books of account are in order.

## Marketing and advertising

In the article referred to earlier, the distinguished jurist remarked:

> A young lawyer once complained to me that he had to work all night to get business and all day to take care of it. In nearly every large firm in our great cities the indispensable partner is “the business getter.”

It is hard to imagine a successful business without clients. To win clients, a business must embrace marketing and advertising, and, like any other business, lawyers too need a marketable product. But lawyers do not have a blank cheque: the Advocates (Marketing and Advertising) Rules, 2014²⁰ set out the strictures within which an Advocate may market a practice.

An Advocate may only advertise²¹ in a non-legal or professional directory; on a website or other digital platform; in the print media (up to four times a year, and no larger than 0.210m × 0.297m); or by a plate or plaque at the entrance to the firm’s ordinary place of business (no larger than 0.5m × 0.35m). An advocate may not advertise on radio, television, or by illuminated billboard or placard.²²

An advocate who attends a conference, seminar or similar public activity may publish a paper, circular or article, but only by identifying that advocate by name and profession.²³

Where advertising is permitted, it may provide only limited information²⁴: the identity of the advocate and firm; the date of admission to the Roll of Advocates; contact details; hours and language of business; and academic or professional qualifications, or contributions to legal education. It may not disclose²⁵ the name or identity of a client; a picture of the advocate or partners; positions held before admission to the Roll; or any promise to achieve a particular outcome.

An Advocate or firm commits professional misconduct, and may be disciplined, for failing to comply with the Rules; using a public appearance for advertisement; using an intermediary to solicit business; or making false or misleading statements to solicit professional business.

The advent of social media has transformed how people find information and services, and the legal profession has not been left behind: increasingly, lawyers market their practices online in creative ways. The time has come for the 2014 Rules to be updated to specifically regulate advertising via social media, which many lawyers have pursued with enthusiasm and verve, at times in ways that amount to unfairly seeking or attracting professional business contrary to the Rules as currently drafted.²⁶

## Charging of fees

Payment of legal fees is regulated by the Advocates (Remuneration) Order, 1962 (the “ARO”). An Advocate is prevented from charging below what the ARO provides; to do so is undercutting, which is an offence.²⁷ An Advocate is also not permitted to share profits from professional business with a non-Advocate; such a person would likewise be guilty of an offence.²⁸

An Advocate and a client may enter into a fee agreement at any point, setting out the Advocate’s remuneration, provided it is not below the ARO threshold;²⁹ such an agreement may be set aside if a Court finds it harsh, unconscionable, exorbitant or unreasonable.³⁰

Certain fee agreements are invalid³¹: the purchase by an advocate of a client’s interest in a suit; agreements relieving an advocate of responsibility for professional negligence; purely contingent “payment only on success” arrangements; agreements to accept less than the ARO remuneration, or more than twenty-five per cent of the general damages recovered (less taxed costs); and dispositions void against the Official Receiver under the Insolvency Act, 2015. In the absence of a fee agreement, an Advocate secures fees by taxing the Bill of Costs in accordance with the ARO.

> Clients are really no judge of a lawyer’s fee. The very best work a lawyer can do for his client is just the kind of work a layman can never appreciate.

## Conclusion

The distinguished jurist’s closing words to the young lawyer leave us with some food for thought:

> When you are as old as I, in a search for the real heroes of the profession, you will not look for them on the Bench, nor necessarily among the successful practitioners, but in the lawyer who, while remaining a student devoted to the philosophy of the law, has been active and uncompromising in his fight against wrong and injustice, shunning law as a business and practising it as a profession. There are such men, considered failures by the Bar, but true at heart to the professional ideal.
notes: Champ S. Andrews, “The Law: A Business or a Profession?” (jstor.org/stable/784941).
Norman Bowie, “The Law: From a Profession to a Business” (core.ac.uk/download/pdf/322560023).
Norman Bowie, The Law: From a Profession to a Business.
Lon Fuller, The Morality of Law 109 (revised ed. 1969).
A central message of Plato’s Republic: that it is never in a person’s interest to be unjust, not even a tyrant.
Cap. 16 of the Laws of Kenya.
See Part III of the Advocates Act.
See Rule 2 of the Advocates (Professional Indemnity) Regulations, 2004.
See Rule 3 of the Advocates (Accounts) Rules, 1966.
Cap. 488 of the Laws of Kenya.
See Rule 2 of the Advocates (Accounts) Rules, 1966.
See Rule 13 of the Advocates (Accounts) Rules, 1966.
Section 36 of the Advocates Act, Cap. 16 of the Laws of Kenya.

posts.title: Discriminatory Taint
posts.author: OOC Advocates
posts.excerpt: When may we call a policy the progeny of an earlier, discriminatory policy, especially if the policies diverge in design and designer? It is an old problem, but its resolution hardly seems impending.
